articles.title: Transparency and trust are the foundations of every successful research partnership, report suggests
articles.description: According to research by the IfM Bonn, strengthening research collaboration between universities and businesses requires regional technology transfer networks in which technology transfer offices at universities and research institutions, as well as chambers of commerce and industry, trade associations, chambers of crafts, business-related networks and financial intermediaries, all play an active role. In this way, networking opportunities could be pooled and examples of good practice highlighted.

articles.title: How high turnover rates in Tanzania's agro-dealer sector affect farmer fertilizer adoption
articles.description: Smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa adopt agricultural inputs, including fertilizer, at low rates, contributing to low agricultural productivity. Previous research has shown that insufficient information and distrust in the quality of products for sale in local markets are among the reasons for low rates of fertilizer adoption and application. In a new study published in the American Journal of Agricultural Economics, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign researchers examined the agricultural marketplace in Tanzania, finding that frequent turnover among local agro-dealers affects farmer perceptions of product quality and has implications for broader market functioning.

articles.title: A new mechanism for reading extra-long genes in neurons
articles.description: Neurons in humans and other mammals express many exceptionally long genes, ranging from more than 100 kbp to more than 2 Mbp, that are important for forming synapses and neural circuits. In general, genetic information is read from DNA into RNA. This process is called transcription. The longer a gene is, the more time it takes to read from beginning to end. In addition, gene expression must be regulated at several steps. Neurons are therefore thought to require special mechanisms to read long genes accurately and stably, but the details of these mechanisms have remained unclear.

articles.title: Study explores new photonics advance: Topology imprinting in nonlinear metasurfaces
articles.description: Light is traditionally described by properties such as wavelength, amplitude, phase and polarization. Advances in optics have shown that light can also be shaped into complex spatial patterns known as structured light, enabling new ways to carry information and interact with matter for applications in imaging, optical communications and information processing.

articles.title: How a pathogen turns flowers into leaves
articles.description: Scientists have found how a protein produced by bacteria disrupts the mechanism that controls flower development in plants, turning reproductive organs into leaf-like structures. These findings shed light on a plant disease that is expected to spread as climate change expands the range of its insect vectors in northern latitudes. They used a synchrotron technique at ESRF, the European Synchrotron in Grenoble, France. The results are an Editor's Pick in the Journal of Biological Chemistry.

articles.title: Smart nanoparticles deliver antibiotics directly to H. pylori
articles.description: Helicobacter pylori bacteria infect around half the global population and are a leading cause of stomach ulcers and gastric cancer. While antibiotics remain the standard treatment, they often fail to reach bacteria hidden beneath the stomach's protective mucus layer and deep within ulcer tissue. This often requires higher antibiotic doses, increasing the risk of adverse effects and antibiotic resistance.

articles.title: Reactions to NFL Opening Weekend 2026
articles.description: As has become almost a yearly tradition, I like to give some of my thoughts and potential overreactions to the opening weekend of the NFL season! In previous iterations, I have done decently well at predicting the landscape of the league, but there are a couple of noteworthy misses, such as entirely overlooking the eventual Super Bowl champions in my early season top-10 power rankings ... hopefully this year I can be a bit more on the money! Southern California Drama Meets Melbourne Madness In one of the most highly anticipated matchups of the year, Thursday Night Football began on a Friday on the other side of the globe! NFC West division rivals San Francisco and Los Angeles faced off at the illustrious Melbourne Cricket Ground in front of over 100,000 people. These two teams could not have had more polar opposite offseasons, one clouded by injuries , shootings and imposter NFL players , while the other added three of the best defensive players in the world , including a (not so shocking) unretirement from one of the sport's greatest . Despite this, it was San Francisco, the underdog, who came out as the dominant victors from this matchup down under. In what many expected to be a coming-out party for the odds-on favorite to win the Super Bowl, the 49ers completely shut down what looked to be a jet-lagged Rams team. Matthew Stafford looked horrible, missing countless throws by wide margins, and the reigning DPOY did not register a single stat. Speaking of which, Garrett has now been put on the IR and is expected to miss at least four weeks with arthroscopic surgery on his knee. Maybe I am too giddy on the upside of the 49ers if they can stay healthy, or maybe I'm being too reactionary towards the Rams, but one of my biggest hot takes this season is that the Niners will win the entire NFC and earn that bye week in the first round of the playoffs. Shanahan has proven countless times that his teams are not to be brushed to the side, and I have full confidence in this revamped San Fran offense with Deebo back in the fold and Mike Evans as the X. Are the Bears This Year's Cowboys? The highest-octane matchup of the week was, by far, the game between the Chicago Bears and the Carolina Panthers , in which there were a combined 96 points scored! The Bears accounted for 59 of those points, in large part due to a Herculean effort on the ground, amassing 291 yards on just 39 carries, along with six touchdowns. Head Coach Ben Johnson did state during the offseason that he wanted the team to have the "highest scoring offense ever," and it's pretty safe to assume he was not joking. However, there is a rather glaring issue that I see with this team, found on the other side of the ball: their defense. Last season the Bears found a lot of success due to an unsustainable amount of turnover luck . Their turnover margin was +22, while the second highest (the Houston Texans, arguably the best defense in the league) was just +17. Now if the Bears had more talent on their roster this might not be such an issue, but with the departures of Gervon Dexter , Kevin Byard , Nahshon Wright and Tremaine Edmunds , it is difficult to see them crack even the top half of the league in most defensive metrics. Like last year's Cowboys who suffered from defensive woes that saw them miss the playoffs, the Bears have all the offensive weaponry required to go head-to-head with every team in the league. However, if they make a habit of poor defensive performances like against Carolina, a sub-par offense, then they too could fall short of the lofty goals they have for themselves. Lamar and Josh are the Best in the Business Following a disappointing year for Lamar Jackson, plagued by injury and offensive woes, the pressure was back on to show that he can still play at an MVP-level. Baltimore fans should be relieved after seeing how he performed, throwing for an efficient 324 yards and adding 40 more on the ground. The Ravens looked scary en route to demolishing the Indianapolis Colts , and in large part due to their superstar quarterback. We cannot forget about his running mate, Derrick Henry, who seems to be getting better with age, rushing for 144 yards and three touchdowns: a superhuman effort from the 32-year-old King. Josh Allen was also sublime in his season debut against what many consider to be the best defense in the league. Allen also finished his 2025 season in disappointing fashion, turning the ball over five times against the Denver Broncos, but he looks in prime shape to make a charge towards his first Super Bowl. Fantasy managers across the country were delighted to see him account for four touchdowns, two through the air and two on the ground, along with 334 passing yards. The two biggest questions surrounding the Bills will once again be their defense and Josh Allen himself limiting turnovers. Those two things killed Buffalo last year, and they'll be hoping that those nightmares don't come back to haunt them in crunch time later this season.

articles.title: Footbridge over Wyman Park's Stony Run reopens
articles.description: The small pedestrian bridge in Wyman Park, over the Stony Run stream, reopened in late August. The bridge is located in the northern part of the park and connects a trail that runs east to west across the park. The trail begins at the end of Craycombe Avenue in the Hampden neighborhood and ends at San Martin Drive, which marks the western edge of Homewood Campus. Stony Run flows north to south throughout Wyman Park, and bridges that cross the stream are limited. The newly-rebuilt footbridge is the closest crossing of the stream to much of the Homewood campus, with the trail letting out near the Bloomberg Center for Physics and Astronomy. Since Wyman Park is located in between Homewood Campus and the Hampden neighborhood, crossing the park is often the most convenient way to get between the two. The footbridge and trail closed in May 2025 because of potential safety concerns. Baltimore City councilwoman Odette Ramos, who represents District 14 - including both Hampden and Homewood Campus - announced over Instagram that the bridge would be closing. "Our engineers are diligently working to resolve the issue with the bridge's structural integrity. Please stay clear of this area. This is for everyone's safety," Ramos announced. Because of the bridge's closure, those passing between Homewood Campus and Hampden had to find alternative ways to travel. The trail remained closed while the bridge was being rebuilt by Baltimore City's Department of Recreation and Parks, until it reopened prior to the start of the academic year. The reopening of the bridge was announced by the conservation organization Friends of Stony Run . On August 25, the organization announced on their website that the bridge was considered safe to cross and that the trail had reopened as well. "We are excited to share that the Craycombe Road Stony Run pedestrian bridge is open again," the organization wrote. While Ramos did not initially share the issues with the bridge's structure, Friends of Stony Run offered more context in their announcement, saying that the bridge had only been temporarily repaired. They are continuing to plan how to replace the bridge permanently. "The failing support structures for the bridge have been reinforced with stacked heavy bags filled with structural grout - allowing the current bridge to be used again temporarily while a permanent replacement is designed. Stay tuned for the next round of improvements and plans for a permanent bridge," the organization wrote. Sophomore Fabiana Arcila, majoring in Biomedical Engineering, worked on campus over the summer and lived in Hampden before the bridge reopened. When asked about her commute to Homewood, she said that she tried many different ways to get to campus more efficiently. "It depended day-to-day, I used kind of a mix. At the beginning, I walked, which was a 30 minute walk from Hampden to AMR II. Then I started taking the Spin scooters," said Arcila. "I also tried taking the shuttle [...] but I missed it all the time." When Arcila did walk, she said that she was able to go through Wyman Park, but sometimes had to bypass it entirely. "It's a very scenic route," said Arcila. "But usually, when it was raining, I wouldn't go through there because it's going to be muddy. So I would take the long route and just walk up and then walk down." When informed of the Stony Run Bridge's reopening, Arcila thought that the bridge would have made her commute much more convenient. "If I had a bridge, that would have made it easier for me to walk," said Arcila.

articles.title: Casting the 007th: Who is the next James Bond?
articles.description: Who is the next Bond, James Bond? Since No Time To Die marked the end of Daniel Craig's tenure in the role, five candidates have repeatedly emerged in recent publications from Page Six to BBC as we wait for the official announcement at the end of this year . But why all this speculation now? The Independent reports that the screenwriter of the upcoming 26th Bond film, Steven Knight (creator of Peaky Blinders ), was recently asked in an interview with BBC Radio 4 about whether he wrote the script with the chosen actor in mind or relied on the already established canon. "It's a bit of both. It does make life a little bit easier if you know who that person is, but also you have to write the character, not the actor," he said. Additionally, actor Gary Oldman, of the TV series Slow Horses , whose co-star has appeared in the running for Bond, addressed the rumors when asked about the James Bond rumors on Canada's The Morning Show . "We're going to find out pretty soon, aren't we? Because they have picked him... They have made their choice, but they have not announced it yet," Oldman said. Since Amazon MGM acquired the Bond franchise from the long-time ownership of the Broccoli family in February 2025, all eyes have been on the talent coming in. Denis Villeneuve (director of the Dune trilogy) is set to direct . Amy Pascal (producer of the Marvel Cinematic Universe's Spiderman franchise and Project Hail Mary ) and David Heyman (producer of Paddington and the Fantastic Beasts franchises) are set to produce . The final piece remains. Here are the frontrunners: No time to die Jacob Elordi is no stranger to Hollywood. He's starred in hits such as Saltburn , Frankenstein (2025) and Wuthering Heights (2026). He's also being set to star in the book-to-screen adaption of Outer Dark with Lily Rose-Depp. The Australian actor has circulated through the James Bond rumor mill for a long time, outlasting names like Idris Elba and Aaron Taylor-Johnson . "I just like that people maybe want to put me in their movies. That makes me really glad," Elordi said in 2023 when Extra asked about the casting rumors. Although he has denied recent questions at The Dog Stars premiere in London, he is still certainly a fan favorite. You only live twice Callum Turner, BAFTA TV award nominee and star of popular films such as Eternity and One Night Only , is another contender. He's also had leading roles in TV shows like Masters of the Air and is set to star in Apple TV's Neuromancer . In this upcoming series, he plays a hacker on the dark web intending to pull off a difficult heist against a corporate empire. The British actor has so far laughed off the speculation and has responded to Esquire . "I'm not going to comment. It's just so loaded, it's just such a loaded thing," Turner said. Never say never again Paul Mescal, the future Paul McCartney in the upcoming Beatles biopics, is another popular choice. He has the range, from playing the son of the most famous fictional gladiator ( Gladiator 2 ) to a complicated father in an indie classic ( Aftersun ). Although the Irish actor is likely tied up in the upcoming four-movie Beatle extravaganza, he is also a popular contender. Vogue Adria reports that after appearing in a Bond casting poll on Digital Spy , Mescal spoke about the role. "Would I play Bond? Yeah? I don't know. If that opportunity ever came up, we'd have a conversation about it... I don't want to say yes or no. I'm a huge fan and will continue to be, regardless." For your eyes only Jack Barton is a newer actor, and out of the five, the most unknown. At 31 years old, his main credits include Heartstopper Forever and Steven Knight's SAS: Rogue Heroes - a TV series about how the British Special Air Service came into being during World War II. Ultimately, it may be his relative mystery that keeps him near the front of the pack as the franchise may be looking for a fresh face. Debbie McWilliams, a now retired casting director who worked on 13 of the last 25 Bond movies and cast Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig, described the role in an interview with The Independent . "We want to know as little about [the actor] personally as possible, because that's what spies are. We don't need to know where he goes shopping or who his parents are or where he lives. We never want to see him at home. And a vital element of the whole thing is his job description. He's licensed to kill, and we have to believe that he can do that. If you don't, then you've lost the audience," McWilliams said. On her majesty's Secret Service Finally, there is Jack Lowden. He is Gary Oldman's co-star on Slow Horses as a demoted MI5 agent on a team of similarly dysfunctional agents to defend England. It's a funny coincidence, and the 98% rating on Rotten Tomatoes for this British spy thriller only seems to fuel the rumors. Beyond the show, he is a relatively unknown actor, fitting the bill of McWilliams' descriptions. As a bonus for the James Bond purists, the actor is Scottish, just like the first Bond actor, Sean Connery. Tomorrow never dies Looking back at the previous Bonds, there is a common trend. While most had few credits to their name before Bond, their addition to the franchise propelled their careers into the spotlight. What fate lies in store for the seventh actor to be granted a license to kill? Note for the purists For the purposes of this article, only six actors who have played in classic Bond films produced by the EON Production company are being referenced. They are, in order: Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig. David Niven in the non-EON 1967 comedy spoof version of Casino Royale does not count.

articles.title: Preventing tidal floods in Venice: a talk by Rafael L. Bras
articles.description: The city of Venice consists of various islands sitting in what is deemed as the Venetian Lagoon . Between these 130 islands lie small bridges that connect the floating areas together as one city. The lagoon consists of inlets connecting the Adriatic Sea to three main openings: Lido, Malamocco and Chioggia. To keep the city of Venice atop the surrounding water, an engineering marvel had to be constructed. On Thursday, Sept. 10, Georgia Institute of Technology (Georgia Tech) School of Civil and Environmental Engineering and School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences professor Rafael L. Bras expanded upon his role as a supervisor during the construction of the Venice Gates, including a discussion of its execution and why this solution was chosen. Bras started by providing a brief recount of Venice's history and how its geographical structure came to existence. "Venice has a history of 1000 years... It became Venice when people from the north of the [Venetian] lagoon moved away from attacks of northern tribes, and in essence settled in these islands... Then [the city] was [a] maritime power and controlled commerce for a long time, all along the Mediterranean." The Venetian Lagoon is amorphous, with many different entrances into the lagoon itself. Bras also highlighted various lines on a map of Venice from the 16th century. The Venetians diverted the rivers because they were a market power. After comparing this map to one from the present day, the diversions remain. Ultimately, these led to entrances, or inlets, into the lagoon. Had the Venetians not acted upon the environment, present day Venice would appear as a vast marshland. "Then the other thing you notice of this lagoon is that it's an engineered environment. Nature does not make straight lines... They diverted the rivers so that sediment would not accumulate. They wanted to throw away the sediment out to the ocean because they didn't want to be invaded by land. They were [a] maritime power. They did not have armies. They had naval power, so they wanted to keep a lagoon to protect them, like a big mold for them in many ways." This allows for a shallow lagoon, in which depths vary from 10 to 17 meters. However, on Nov. 4, 1966, intense flooding from the Arno River swept into Florence; a similar event occurred in Venice. The tide reached extreme heights, going over the seawall and over the barrier islands, even breaching some of them. This was a high tide of 0.5 to 0.6 meters over the period of the event. With the combined effect of another meteorological surge, it created a record flood level of approximately two meters. Bras then explained the concepts that are generally attributed to furthering the issue. "There are two elements that [have] created the problem. One is sea level rising... and one is subsidence; the whole lagoon environment sinks." According to Bras, the rate of sinking has accelerated historically especially due to reconstruction of the World Wars, where water was pumped for use by industrial regions. The lagoon has been subsiding at a rate of 0.4 millimeters per year. The rate of sea level increase has accelerated to around 2.7 millimeters per year, almost six times larger than the subsidence. In addition, the number of meteorological events that cause flooding have increased. To solve these issues, an international contest was held for engineers and architects to come up with solutions. "The solution, the best way to solve the problem, is to create a series of barriers that will close off the lagoon from the sea [when you predict a storm surge]. You predict the tide, you close the inlet, keep the ocean out, keep the lagoon down. Ocean can go up. Everything [is] good when everything is over. You open the barriers, and that's it." Bras outlined how this is not a new solution. In Rotterdam, Netherlands, there are also floodgates that when a flood is predicted, they cut off the canal and create a temporary dam. However, this type of gate was not acceptable for the Venetians. They are sizable and too obvious. Venetians wanted something that was able to conserve land, not alter the cross section of the inlet, and be invisible. What Venice decided on were flaps . These large, "invisible" flaps sit under water in a crater, usually full of water. When a meteorological event is predicted, water is pumped out and the flaps float up and rotate around a hinge to create a barrier. Each flap is independent of one another, with a gap of about 15 centimeters between. The gates can open within 20 minutes, compared to Rotterdam's six hours. "This is the way it would operate. It's sitting on its cradle. You pump air out. They come out. They settle in. The sea goes up to wherever it goes. Creates a dam. Goes down the sea. When everything is level, you put water in, air in, and settle [back down] again." There are four sets of gates: Lido North, Lido South, Malamocco and Chioggia. The largest in weight are in Malamocco, which is the industrial hub of the area; the smallest is Lido North. The building of these structures required immense effort. Generally, the gates run from one end of the inlet to the other, closing off access to the land it encloses. In addition, refuge harbors were built for ships that may be stuck outside the barrier in case of a meteorological event. Essentially, the gates were floated to their location, sunk, and then joined. "When the gates operate... the idea is that you make a prediction of the tidal flooding, and you predict that the tide is going to go above some level. The trigger in the operating rules of this is that you trigger a closure when you predict 110 centimeters." Bras then transitioned to another history lesson of the gates, dating back to 1984, when the concept was introduced. At this time, a special law was also made where a consortium named the Consorio Venezia Nuova gained power to protect Venice and the lagoon. Construction started in 2003 and was set to be completed in 2012. However, also at this time, corruption was rampant, including bribing and illegal financing. In addition to the economic crisis of 2008, funding to complete the project was low. The Italian government also fired individuals involved with the project, which left no experts to carry out the rest of construction. In 2020, the government decided to resume construction and eventually the gates were operational by 2021. Bras emphasized that although they were operational, there still was a change in how these gates were functioning. "The big difference is that this is being operated manually because the automatic controls were all gone." Bras finished his lecture providing some images of a flooded Venice. He used these photos to illustrate that with the gates now in successful operation, the future of Venice is dry.

articles.title: Willem Dafoe's lost poet navigates integrity in Late Fame
articles.description: Performance runs central in critic-turned-filmmaker Kent Jones' sophomore feature film Late Fame . Aside from the masterful performances of the talented leads, Willem Dafoe and Greta Lee, the story depicts the wayward identity of being an intellectual writer and the resulting lack of sincerity in performing for others. Written by screenwriter Samy Burch , of May December and Coyote vs. Acme fame, the script adapts Arthur Schnitzler's novella of the same name from a late 19th-century Austrian setting into a contemporary New York portrait of vast class and generational differences amid the continuous pursuit of art. In downtown Manhattan, Ed Saxberger (Willem Dafoe) lives as an aging, elderly postal office worker who seems content playing pool with his working class friends in his spare time. One day, he's approached by Meyers (Edmund Donovan), a wealthy NYU graduate, who expresses great awe and reverence towards Saxberger. Meyers explains he's obsessed with Saxberger's mostly forgotten, unacclaimed poetry collection from the '70s: Way Past Go . Meyers invites Saxberger to meet his literary group of young, rich writers called "The Enthusiasm Society," claiming they're also fellow fervent admirers of Saxberger's writing. Saxberger agrees, and he's quickly fond of the attention he receives from the group. He's particularly drawn by Gloria (Greta Lee), the only member of the group who's an actress. As he gets more involved with the members of The Enthusiasm Society, he discovers there's less he has in common with the writers and their goals than he initially expects. At one point, Saxberger describes Meyers as an "Edith Wharton protagonist." When Saxberger visits Meyers' massive apartment in the city, he confirms his comparison. Meyers is a truly wealthy upper-class man from a family providing significant monetary support. He shows off his first edition of Naked Lunch , which Saxberger opens to see a price tag of $1,200 inside. Later, he sets Saxberger up to meet with a literary agent who's a family friend of Meyers. Despite all of Meyers' institutional credentials, like a MFA from a prestigious university and deep connections to the publishing world, he seems superficially interested in actually writing. While Saxberger struggles to overcome writer's block in writing a new poetry collection for publication, Meyers' primary goals are expanding the cultural reach of The Enthusiasm Society; he offers no genuine sympathy towards Saxberger when the older man confides in him about the difficulties of writing poetry again. While the friendship between Meyers and Saxberger starts to deteriorate, Gloria and Saxberger grow closer. Saxberger realizes Gloria's performances have extended beyond the flirty actor persona she has. Unlike the other wealthy members of the Enthusiasm Society, Gloria, like Saxberger, lives with ordinary, working-class means. He finds Gloria in her regular, almost bare-bones apartment where she's unadorned by any elaborate makeup or costumes. The two get into a disagreement as she urges him to leave, unhappy to be seen in this state of sincerity. Now, all his major relationships within The Enthusiasm Society seem strained. And earlier, before this confrontation with Gloria, Saxberger had abruptly left his pool-playing friends after attempting to share his poetry with them; his poetry was not received with proper consideration or respect. Saxberger reacts coldly to this reception, and his friends fight back too. They argue that Saxberger must think they're too "low-brow" for him. Eventually, the reading event Meyers has planned with The Enthusiasm Society comes to pass. Saxberger reads his own poetry to a crowd and Gloria also performs some of his work. The poetry reading gets mostly negative reviews, and Saxberger must navigate the group's response and his own future as a poet. Willem Dafoe imbues a delicate quality of subtle joy and sadness in his performance. His superb portrayal of Saxberger's resilience and wisdom makes the poet's moments of vulnerability much more impactful. Similarly, Greta Lee conveys all of Gloria's nuances with appropriate depth; a glamorous actress, a struggling woman in the city and a dreamer who follows opportunity. Although Late Fame tackles the class and generational differences between its characters, the film's most lasting interrogation dissects the performances of all its players. As Meyers, Gloria and Saxberger accept or reject the expectations given to them, they reveal the ever-changing motives for portraying or hiding parts of their identity as an artist. Saxberger, in particular, discovers the crucial need to be true to your pursuits. After being involved in the tumultuous dynamics of the wealthy literary youth, Saxberger plays pool again with his old friends by the end of the movie. His career in poetry may have never truly actualized, but he knows who he is.

articles.title: The foundational abilities requirements are failing humanities students
articles.description: I am a member of the first Hopkins class for which the completion of the Foundational Ability (FA) credits has been mandatory for students in the Krieger School of Arts and Sciences (KSAS). Throughout my time here, I have heard many compelling arguments - some of which have appeared in The News-Letter before - against the restrictive liberal arts requirements, especially drawing on the history of Hopkins as a specialized research institution. These arguments are compelling, though slightly incomplete. Most of the prior pleas for the system's repeal have come from STEM students forced to take humanities courses. This is natural, as certain humanities departments -like International Studies, my own major - have pre-existing requirements that already demand students take courses that span the current FAs. Despite this, the influx of STEM majors into humanities classes, degrading the quality of discussion-based humanities courses, has made the FAs just as harmful to non-STEM majors within KSAS. Having diverse perspectives is incredibly important and rightfully celebrated at Hopkins and other elite institutions. Even so, there are certain situations in which the ability of a STEM major to contribute in a humanities class based on their unique lived experience is reliant on their willingness to do so, which FA requirements interfere with. During my freshman year, two of my floormates, both of whom were pre-med STEM majors in KSAS, took Introduction to Fiction and Poetry (IFP) in order to fulfill their FA1 Writing and Communication requirement. Throughout the semester, I watched idly as they continuously used ChatGPT to produce poetry. Beyond my concerns for their personal development, I wondered how this was impacting the quality of class discussion and participation -surely they were not the only STEM students using the introductory Writing Seminars class as an easy way to fulfill their requirements. Later on, in The News-Letter Gatehouse, I asked some fellow editors about their experiences in IFP as humanities majors; they affirmed my assumption that discussions were often filled with uninformed and uninspired contributions by non-Writing Seminars majors. On top of that, they expressed difficulty registering for the class in the first place, which is necessary for their major, due to the increased demand. This conundrum indicates that, instead of inspiring interdisciplinary exploration and the expansion of the breadth of undergraduates' knowledge, fulfilling the FAs is an annoying chore for STEM students and a hurdle to deeper learning for humanities students. In the current age of technology, STEM students naturally employ AI and other forms of academic dishonesty to complete this chore, further weakening the quality of the humanities courses they choose. The aspect of this issue that is unique to the humanities is twofold. First, humanities majors are more likely to be able to fulfill their FAs within the realm of their own majors - as an International Studies and History major, I have not been forced to explore beyond my existing major requirements in order to fulfill my FA credits. Because of this, humanities students who are less familiar with general STEM concepts are not populating introductory STEM courses against their will. The second issue is that, because many upper-level courses in the humanities do not require prerequisites - something more common among STEM courses - STEM students also populate upper-level courses. The phenomenon of having STEM students without humanities backgrounds or relevant experience in upper-level humanities courses is something I am intimately familiar with. During this semester alone, I have enrolled in both 200- and 300-level History courses with significant populations of STEM students who openly admit that they have chosen the courses simply to fulfill a requirement. I can only assume that this is why the professors of these courses go on to assure the class that no prior experience is needed to succeed. Hearing such comments is what inspired me to write this piece in the first place. Previously, I accepted TAs having to explain the foundational elements of Rousseau's philosophy, the Opium Wars, or the Articles of Confederation as a painful but inevitable fact of life. In hearing professors, especially in upper-level courses, assert that no prior knowledge of history is necessary for the class, I began to wonder whether the quality of my education was being impacted by the necessity for STEM students to take humanities courses, and whether their syllabi had been edited since STEM students flooded into their classes on account of the FA system. If 3 of 15 necessary credits in the Science and Data FA2 requirement can apply to Elements of Microeconomics, a requirement for an International Studies major , there is no reason that a given course in, for example, the Medicine, Science, and Humanities department cannot also be tagged with the Culture and Aesthetics FA3. Separately, the reason humanities students are not fulfilling their FAs by taking, for example, Physical Chemistry I , a 300-level Chemistry course, is not only because they can fulfill their requirements elsewhere in a more relevant field - it's because they are systematically prevented from doing so. In this way, the system recognizes that admitting humanities students to upper-level STEM courses would naturally interfere with the efficiency and rigor of the course and uses pre-requisites to prevent that. Why is the same principle not applied to the humanities? The University therefore has three options if it decides to rectify this issue: cross-list more STEM courses with more humanities-related FAs so that students can use relevant coursework to fulfill them; create explicit prerequisites for humanities courses; or abandon the FA project entirely. The blame does not lie with the STEM student. It lies only with the University, which failed to consider the decreased rigor of humanities courses that are natural when the FA system is implemented in its current form. Those costs are not worth the appearance of offering a more liberal arts-based education to onlookers while students pay. Julia Schager is a junior majoring in International Studies and History from Stamford, Conn.She is a Copy Editor for The News-Letter .
